title: What Is Seat Spinning? How Bots Distort Airline Demand Data & How to Stop Them
summary:
A flight shows sold out. Hours before departure, seats reappear. Nothing was refunded, so what happened?

Often, bots. They hold seats, never pay, and let the hold expire. Your demand data turns to noise, fares climb, and real travelers book elsewhere.

Key takeaways

  • Seat spinning is a bot attack in which automated scripts place airline seats on hold, never pay, and let the holds expire before starting over. Unauthorized resellers use it to resell seats at a markup, and competitors use it to block real customers from buying.
  • Every step of a spin, from search to seat selection to hold, is a valid booking action, so WAFs and CAPTCHAs let it through. The abuse only shows up in the sequence.
  • Seat spinning distorts look-to-book ratios and demand data, makes flights look fuller than they are, and can push fares up, sending travelers to resellers or competitors.
  • To check for seat spinning in your own data, compare hold-to-ticket ratios by session, IP, and device, then look for repeat holds on the same flight and flights that reopen after selling out.
  • Stopping seat spinning requires intent-based detection, which allows you to block malicious automation without adding friction for real travelers.

title: Meta’s Muse Now Signs as Muse.ai: What an AI Agent’s Identity Switch Means for Web Bot Auth
summary:
Over one weekend, Muse moved its cryptographic signatures from Meta’s key directory to its own. It’s a small change in an HTTP header, and a big signal for how AI agents will identify themselves on the web.

TL;DR

  • Muse, Meta’s agentic browser, now signs some of its requests with its own Web Bot Auth key directory, muse.ai, instead of Meta’s meta.com.
  • The handover was gradual: it started around midnight PST on Saturday, November 7, ran at roughly 50/50 for a day and a half, and was complete on Monday, November 9.
  • Muse’s signed traffic held its level throughout the switch.
  • If you verify Web Bot Auth signatures and only trust meta.com, Muse’s requests now look unverified to you.

A quick refresher: What Web Bot Auth does

Web Bot Auth lets an automated client prove who it is. The agent signs each HTTP request with a private key using HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) and adds a Signature-Agent header pointing to a public key directory, hosted at /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory on the agent operator’s domain. Anyone receiving the request can fetch the public keys and check the signature.
